lessons.title: Build squares and find square roots
ideas: A square number counts dots in equal rows and columns.
A square root asks how many dots are in one row.
The principal square root is non-negative, even though both signs can solve a square equation.

examples.question: Find $\sqrt{324}$ by prime factorisation.
steps: Take one factor from every pair: $2\times3^2=18$.

examples.question: Show that the sum of the first six odd positive integers is a square.
steps: Six L-shaped borders make a 6 by 6 square.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Add the next L-shaped border of 9 counters.
experiment.result: The new square has 25 counters: consecutive squares differ by odd numbers.

lessons.title: Build cubes and find cube roots
ideas: A cube has three equal edge lengths.
A cube number counts small cubes in equal layers.
A cube root undoes cubing; a negative number has a negative real cube root.

examples.question: Find the cube root of 1728.
A cube is made from 343 unit cubes. Find its edge, then the number of unit cubes in its bottom layer.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Build a 2 by 2 layer with blocks.
experiment.result: There are 8 blocks: 2 cubed is 8.

lessons.title: Prime groups and perfect powers
ideas: For a perfect square every prime occurs in pairs.
For a perfect cube every prime occurs in triples.
To complete a square or cube, supply only the missing prime factors.

examples.question: Find the smallest positive integer by which 72 must be multiplied to make a square.
steps: The power of 2 is odd; supply one more 2.

examples.question: Find the least positive integer by which 108 must be divided to obtain a perfect cube.
steps: Remove the two factors of 2: divide by 4.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
experiment.result: One unpaired 2 shows why multiplying by 2 makes 144, a square.

lessons.title: Use a square model in a real situation
ideas: Area uses square units; side length uses ordinary units.
Read whether a question asks for area, edge or number of objects.
Check by squaring or cubing the proposed root.

examples.question: Without multiplying fully, find the difference between the squares of 31 and 30.
steps: This is the next odd border.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain

Find a whole-number side that produces this area.

ideas: In a power the base is repeated; the exponent counts factors.

lessons.title: Combine powers with the same base
ideas: Multiplication joins lists of equal factors.
Division cancels equal factors, provided the denominator is non-zero.
A power raised to a power multiplies the exponents.

lessons.title: Zero and negative exponents
ideas: Descending powers divide by the base at every step.
The zero power of a non-zero base is 1.
A negative exponent means reciprocal; it does not mean a negative value.

examples.question: Write $\frac{1}{125}$ as a power of 5.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain

lessons.title: Powers of ten in measurements

Large quantities have positive powers of ten; tiny quantities have negative powers.
Track units and the number of decimal moves.

g8-story-numbers.title: A Story of Numbers
g8-story-numbers.subtitle: NCERT Ganita Prakash Part 1 · Chapter 3 · Start from basics; build confidence one step at a time

lessons.title: Why place value matters
ideas: The same digit has different values in different positions.
A place-value system needs a placeholder for an empty place.
Zero represents no units in a place; it is not always removable.

examples.question: Write 60,307 in expanded form.
steps: Keep the empty thousands and tens places in mind.

examples.question: Explain why 205 and 25 do not have the same value.
steps: The zero holds the tens position.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Build 204 using hundreds, tens and ones cards.
Remove the zero card and read 24.
experiment.result: The zero kept the hundreds and ones in their correct places.

lessons.title: Compare ways to write numbers
ideas: An additive numeral adds the values of its symbols.
A positional numeral uses both a symbol and its location.
We can compare systems without claiming one historical method works exactly like another.

Egyptian numerals used repeated powers-of-ten symbols; Roman notation also uses subtractive pairs such as IV. Babylonian place value grouped in base 60; Mayan positional notation commonly grouped in base 20 and used a zero sign. Indian decimal positional notation made ten-place grouping and zero especially powerful. These systems developed over long periods and have different conventions.

examples.question: Compare Roman XIV and decimal14. How does each represent the same quantity?
steps: Roman X contributes10, and IV is the subtractive pair4.
The decimal numeral14 means one ten and four ones.
They name the same amount with different notation rules.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Write a small number with tally marks.
Write it again with decimal digits.
experiment.result: Place value uses fewer marks for large quantities.

lessons.title: Group in bases
ideas: Base ten groups ten units into the next place.
In base two, digits can only be 0 and 1, and places are powers of 2.
Always state the base when a representation could be ambiguous.

examples.question: Convert binary 1101 to decimal.
Write decimal 19 in binary.
Convert base-five numeral 234 to decimal.
steps: All digits are smaller than base 5.

examples.question: Represent decimal 37 in base five and verify.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Group 13 counters into groups of 8, 4, 2 and 1.
experiment.result: 13 is 1101 in base two.

lessons.title: Explain a representation
ideas: Read from the highest place to the lowest.
Multiply each digit by its place value, then add.
Use a reverse conversion to check your answer.

examples.question: A decimal three-digit number has hundreds digit 4, tens digit 0 and ones digit 7. Reverse the digits and compare.
steps: The number is 407; its reversal is 704.

examples.question: In the place-value display: (a) add the occupied binary places; (b) represent decimal 14 in binary.
steps: The occupied places 8, 2 and 1 add to 11.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
experiment.result: Both the diagram and the decimal value describe the same quantity.

diagram.caption: A binary place-value display has columns 8, 4, 2 and 1; digits 1, 0, 1 and 1 occupy these columns.

g8-quadrilaterals.title: Quadrilaterals
g8-quadrilaterals.subtitle: NCERT Ganita Prakash Part 1 · Chapter 4 · Start from basics; build confidence one step at a time

lessons.title: Name four-sided shapes
ideas: A quadrilateral is a simple closed polygon with four sides.
Draw a diagonal to split it into two triangles.
The four interior angles total 360 degrees.

examples.question: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 80°, 95° and 105°. Find the fourth.
A quadrilateral has angles x, 2x, 3x and 4x. Find all angles and check their total.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Join one pair of opposite vertices.
experiment.result: The two triangles each contribute 180 degrees.

lessons.title: Parallelograms
ideas: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel.
Opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles are supplementary.
Its diagonals bisect each other; they need not be equal.

examples.question: One angle of a parallelogram is 65°. Find all four angles.
Diagonals of a parallelogram intersect at O. If AO=4.5 cm and BO=3 cm, find AC and BD.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Fold or trace its diagonals and mark their intersection.
experiment.result: Each diagonal is divided into two equal halves.

lessons.title: Rectangles, rhombi and squares
ideas: A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles.
A rhombus is a parallelogram with equal sides.
A square has both properties; its diagonals are equal and perpendicular.
A kite has two pairs of adjacent equal sides. Its diagonal through the vertices between equal-side pairs is a symmetry axis in a non-rhombus kite.
A trapezium has a pair of opposite parallel sides. Some books reserve this name for exactly one pair; use the convention in a question.

examples.question: A rhombus has perimeter 36 cm. Find its side and explain why its shape is not fixed by this alone.
steps: Different angles can give different rhombi with side 9 cm.
examples.result: 9 cm; an angle or diagonal is also needed to fix the shape.

examples.question: Explain why every square is a rectangle but not every rectangle is a square.
steps: A square has four right angles, so it satisfies the rectangle definition.
A rectangle need not have all sides equal.
A 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle is a counterexample.
examples.result: The square family is contained in the rectangle family.

examples.question: In kite ABCD, AB=AD and BC=CD. Prove that angles ABC and ADC are equal.
steps: Join AC; it is a common side.
Triangles ABC and ADC have three corresponding side pairs equal, so SSS applies.
Their corresponding B and D angles are equal.
examples.result: The opposite angles between unequal side pairs are equal.

examples.question: AB is parallel to CD in trapezium ABCD. If angle A=75°, find angle D.
steps: A and D are interior angles on the same side of AD.
examples.result: 105°. Givens, rather than the drawing, establish parallelism.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Make a table of sides, angles and diagonals.
Place a square in both the rectangle and rhombus columns.
experiment.result: Special shapes can belong to more than one family.

lessons.title: Use properties with reasons
ideas: Mark equal sides and parallel arrows on a diagram.
Select a property before forming an equation.
A slanted sketch can still represent a rectangle; measurements and given properties decide.

examples.question: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are x and 2x. Find them.
For parallelogram ABCD shown: (a) find B and C; (b) if AC=12 cm, find AO and OC.
steps: O is the intersection of the diagonals.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain

experiment.result: Its angles are 70, 110, 70 and 110 degrees.

ideas: A pattern is useful only when its rule is stated.
Check a proposed rule on every given example.

examples.question: Prove that the sum of two consecutive integers is odd.
steps: This is one more than an even number.

examples.question: Show that the product of consecutive integers is even.

steps: List odd and even numbers on cards.
Combine two cards of each parity.
experiment.result: Even plus even and odd plus odd are even; odd plus even is odd.

lessons.title: Divisibility and remainders
ideas: A divisibility test follows from place value.
Digit sums test divisibility by 3 and 9.

examples.question: Use a digit test to decide whether 738 is divisible by 9.
Use the divisibility test for 11 on 2728.
steps: 11 is divisible by 11, so 2728 is also divisible by 11.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain

experiment.result: 123 and 1+2+3 leave the same remainder on division by 9.

lessons.title: Reverse digits and use letters
ideas: Represent a two-digit number as 10a+b.
Its reversal is 10b+a.
Subtracting reveals a multiple of 9 without trying every number.

examples.question: Find the missing digit in 4x2 so that the number is divisible by 9.
steps: For a digit from 0 to 9, the only possible multiple of 9 is 9.

examples.question: A two-digit number has digit sum 11. It is 27 greater than its reversal. Find it.

steps: In the ones column,7+B ends in5, so7+B=15 and B=8, carrying1.
In the tens column,A+3+1=6, so A=2.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Choose a two-digit number with different non-zero digits.
Subtract its reversal from the larger numeral.
experiment.result: The difference is a multiple of 9.

lessons.title: Patterns in arrays
ideas: An array turns a product into rows and columns.
Check whether a grouping uses every object with no remainder.
Use variables to justify a pattern rather than relying on a picture alone.

sheet.title: Percent means out of one hundred

lessons.title: Percent means out of one hundred
ideas: Percent is another way of naming a fraction.
Divide by 100 to convert a percent to a number.
To express a ratio as percentages, compare each part to the total.

examples.question: Express 3 out of 8 as a percentage.
In the shaded strip: (a) express the shaded fraction as a percentage; (b) if it represents ₹600 of a budget, find the total budget.
steps: Three of four equal parts are shaded, so $\frac34=75\%$.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Divide the whole hundred-square grid into four groups of25 squares.
Shade exactly one of these groups.
experiment.result: 25 percent is one quarter of the whole grid.

diagram.caption: Three quarters of a budget are shaded. The shaded amount is ₹600.

lessons.title: Find amounts and reverse percentages
ideas: A percent must refer to a particular whole.
To find a percentage of an amount, multiply by the corresponding fraction.
To recover the original amount, divide by that fraction.

examples.question: Find the number whose 35% is 140.
A quantity rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. Explain the net change with an example.
steps: Begin with 100; after the rise it is 120.
20% of 120 is 24, so the final value is 96.
The loss from the original is 4 out of 100.
examples.result: A net decrease of 4%, not zero.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
experiment.result: 20 counters are 25 percent of 80, not 25 percent of 20.

lessons.title: Profit, loss, discount and tax
ideas: Profit and loss percentages use cost price as their base.
A discount uses marked price as its base.
Apply tax to the stated taxable price; do successive changes one at a time.

examples.question: An article costs ₹800 and sells for ₹920. Find the profit percentage.
steps: Use cost price 800 as the base.

examples.question: A ₹1,500 item has a 20% discount, then 5% tax on its discounted price. Find the bill.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Reduce it by 10 percent, then raise the reduced price by 10 percent.
experiment.result: The result is ₹99 because the second percentage uses a smaller base.

lessons.title: Simple and compound interest
ideas: Simple interest is calculated on the original principal each year.
Compound interest adds each period’s interest before the next period.
Convert months into years when using an annual simple-interest rate.

examples.question: Find simple interest on ₹2,400 at 8% per year for 9 months.
Find compound interest on ₹5,000 at 10% annually for 2 years.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Compare ₹1,000 at 10 percent for two years.
For simple interest use ₹100 each year; for annual compound interest use ₹100 then ₹110.
experiment.result: The totals are ₹1,200 and ₹1,210.

steps: 25 out of100 reduces by25 to one quarter.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: 15% of 200 is Options: A: 30; B: 15; C: 20; D: 300.
steps: Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: Profit percentage is calculated on Options: A: cost price; B: selling price; C: marked price; D: discount.
steps: Profit is the gain compared with the amount paid to acquire the item.
Therefore the correct choice is cost price.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: ₹1,000 at 10% compounded annually becomes after 2 years Options: A: ₹1,210; B: ₹1,200; C: ₹1,100; D: ₹1,020.
steps: First-year amount1100 earns110 in year two.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

g8-pythagoras.title: The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem
g8-pythagoras.subtitle: NCERT Ganita Prakash Part 2 · Chapter 2 · Start from basics; build confidence one step at a time

lessons.title: Identify the hypotenuse
ideas: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side.
The square areas on the two shorter sides add to the square area on the hypotenuse.
The theorem applies to right triangles, not all triangles.

examples.question: Find the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 9 cm and 12 cm.
steps: Take the positive root because length is positive.

diagram.caption: A right triangle has perpendicular legs9 cm and12 cm. Find the unknown hypotenuse.

examples.question: Determine whether sides 8, 15 and 17 form a right triangle.
examples.result: Yes; the angle opposite side 17 is right.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Draw a 3-4-5 right triangle on squared paper.
Build squares outward on its sides.
experiment.result: 9+16=25 verifies the area relationship in this example.

lessons.title: Find a missing side
ideas: Square first, then add or subtract, then take a root.
If the hypotenuse is missing, add the leg squares.
If a leg is missing, subtract from the hypotenuse square.

examples.question: A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 cm and one leg 5 cm. Find the other leg.
A 10 m ladder has its foot 6 m from a vertical wall. Find its height on the wall.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Use a 5-unit hypotenuse and a 3-unit leg.
experiment.result: It is 25−9=16, so the missing leg is 4.

lessons.title: Triples and the converse
ideas: Three positive integers forming a right triangle are a Pythagorean triple.
To test sides, square the longest first.
An exact equality proves a right angle; a sketch or rounded equality does not.

examples.question: A rectangular field is 24 m by 10 m. Compare walking along two adjacent sides with walking diagonally.
For the right-triangle ramp shown: (a) verify its lengths; (b) find the cost of covering the sloping surface 2 m wide at ₹50 per square metre.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
experiment.result: Multiplying all sides preserves the right angle.

diagram.caption: A ramp forms a right triangle with vertical height 6 m, horizontal run 8 m and sloping length 10 m.

lessons.title: Diagonals, square roots and applications
ideas: A square diagonal forms a right triangle with equal legs.
A unit square has diagonal square root of 2.
A ladder, ramp or diagonal route needs the right-angle assumption labelled.

examples.question: Find the exact diagonal of a square of side 7 cm.
steps: Keep the exact root unless asked to round.

examples.question: Show that $1.41<\sqrt2<1.42$.
steps: Squaring is increasing on non-negative numbers.
examples.result: The positive square root lies strictly between 1.41 and 1.42.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Measure its diagonal approximately, then compare 1.4² and 1.5².
experiment.result: The diagonal lies between 1.4 and 1.5, and is exactly square root of 2.

examples.question: In a right triangle, the longest side is the Options: A: hypotenuse; B: altitude always; C: shorter leg; D: median always.
steps: The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse.
Therefore the correct choice is hypotenuse.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: Legs 6 and 8 give hypotenuse Options: A: 10; B: 14; C: 7; D: 100.
steps: Compare this with the other options before moving on.

steps: Compare this with the other options before moving on.

steps: Compare this with the other options before moving on.

sheet.title: Ratios in maps and three-part mixtures

lessons.title: Ratios in maps and three-part mixtures
ideas: A map scale compares matching lengths in the same units.
A three-term ratio must keep all three quantities in order.
Find the total number of parts before sharing a whole.

examples.question: Divide ₹1,200 in ratio 2:3:5.
A map has scale 1:25,000. Find the actual distance for 4 cm.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
experiment.result: The shares are 12,18 and 30.

lessons.title: Pie charts are proportions of a full turn
ideas: The whole circle is 360 degrees.
Multiply each category fraction by 360.
All sectors must add to 360 degrees and all percentages to 100.

examples.question: In a survey, 18 of 60 students choose cycling. Find its pie-chart angle.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Draw a circle and mark one quarter.
experiment.result: One quarter of 360 degrees is 90 degrees.

lessons.title: Inverse proportion
ideas: When the same job is shared by equally efficient workers, more workers take less time.
For inverse proportion the product is constant.
Do not apply this rule if the job or worker efficiency changes.

examples.question: Six identical pumps empty a tank in 8 hours. How long would 4 take?
A car travels 240 km. Compare the travel times at 60 km/h and 80 km/h.
steps: For fixed distance, speed times time is constant.
examples.result: 4 hours and 3 hours; a saving of 1 hour.

examples.question: The recipe bars show red:blue=3:5: (a) scale to 40 total units; (b) if 5 workers prepare that batch in 6 hours, how long do 3 equal workers take?
steps: Eight parts share 40 units, so one part is 5.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Use 12 counters to represent a job.
experiment.result: Each worker receives 6,4 and 3 units of work.

diagram.caption: A recipe uses red and blue ingredients in ratio 3:5. Identical workers prepare a fixed batch.

lessons.title: Combine work rates
ideas: A work rate is the fraction of a job completed per unit time.
Add rates when workers cooperate independently.
Taking the reciprocal of the combined rate gives completion time.

examples.question: A can finish a job in 6 days; B in 3 days. How long do they take together?
steps: Rates are $\frac16$ and $\frac13$ jobs per day.

examples.question: A and B complete a job in 4 and 12 hours respectively. They work together for 2 hours. What fraction remains?

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Let one worker do a half-job per hour and another a third-job per hour.
experiment.result: Together they do five-sixths of the job per hour.

examples.question: At scale 1:50,000, 2 cm represents Options: A: 1 km; B: 100 km; C: 10 m; D: 100 m.
steps: Therefore the correct choice is 1 km.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: A quarter of a pie chart has angle Options: A: 90°; B: 25°; C: 180°; D: 45°.
steps: One quarter of a360° turn is90°.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: For fixed work, workers and time are usually Options: A: inversely proportional; B: directly proportional; C: equal; D: unrelated always.
steps: With a fixed job, workers×time is constant at equal rates.
Therefore the correct choice is inversely proportional.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

g8-geometric-themes.title: Exploring Some Geometric Themes
g8-geometric-themes.subtitle: NCERT Ganita Prakash Part 2 · Chapter 4 · Start from basics; build confidence one step at a time

sheet.title: Find a shortest path on a surface

lessons.title: Repeated rules make fractals
ideas: A fractal repeats a structure at different scales.
At every Sierpinski triangle step, keep three of four equal smaller triangles.
A finite drawing illustrates a repeated rule; it is not the completed infinite fractal.

examples.question: Find the number of retained triangles after 3 Sierpinski steps.
steps: Each retained triangle produces three new retained triangles.

examples.question: A triangle has area 64 cm². Find the retained area after two Sierpinski steps.
steps: The removed area is 28 square centimetres.

examples.question: For a Sierpinski carpet, one central ninth is removed at each step. Find the retained fraction after two steps.
steps: After two steps the fraction is $\frac89\times\frac89$.

examples.question: Each Koch-curve segment is replaced by four segments one-third as long. Find the perimeter multiplier after two stages.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Draw a triangle and join side midpoints.
Remove the central triangle; repeat on the three corner triangles.
experiment.result: The number of kept triangles triples while total area is multiplied by three quarters.

lessons.title: Nets fold into solids
ideas: A net is a connected arrangement of faces that folds without overlaps.
A cube has six square faces, twelve edges and eight vertices.
Not every six-square arrangement is a cube net.

examples.question: Describe a cube net and explain how to test it.
steps: One valid net has four squares in a row, with one above and one below the second square.
Cut and fold along shared edges.
All six faces must close without overlap.
examples.result: A successful fold verifies this arrangement as a cube net.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Cut a six-square cross net with tabs.
Fold and test whether every face meets correctly.
experiment.result: A real fold is a useful check for overlap and missing faces.

lessons.title: Views and isometric drawings
ideas: Top, front and side views show different information.
A hidden cube may appear in one view but not another.
An isometric drawing represents three directions with a consistent scale; apparent angles are not measured solid angles.

examples.question: A stack has three cubes in the bottom row and one cube directly above its middle cube. Give its front-view column heights and cube count.
steps: The left, middle and right columns have heights 1,2,1.
Add these because the stack is only one cube deep.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Build a stack of unit cubes.
Draw its top, front and right views.
experiment.result: More than one stack can sometimes share the same views.

lessons.title: Find a shortest path on a surface
ideas: A straight line is shortest in an unfolded plane.
Try valid unfoldings, then compare their straight-line lengths.
The shortest surface route is not usually a space diagonal through the solid.

examples.question: A cuboid has sides 3,4,12 cm. Find the shortest surface route between opposite vertices.
For the cuboid-net idea: (a) state the face, edge and vertex counts for a cube; (b) a 3×4×12 cuboid is unfolded with width 3+4 and height 12. Find that route length.
steps: A cube has 6 faces,12 edges,8 vertices.
The chosen rectangle has width 7 and height 12.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Flatten two adjacent rectangular faces of a box.
Draw a straight route between opposite corners.
experiment.result: Refolding gives a straight-on-the-net route along the surface.

diagram.caption: Unfolding adjacent faces of a cuboid turns a surface-path problem into a rectangle-diagonal problem. The illustrative solid is not drawn to scale.

lessons.title: Check your understanding
ideas: Try each question on paper before reading its solution.
Explain why the other options fail: a correct choice is stronger when you can justify it.
If you get stuck, return to the session named in the contents; change one number and try again.

examples.question: The first Sierpinski removal keeps what fraction of a triangle? Options: A: $\frac34$; B: $\frac14$; C: $\frac12$; D: $1$.
steps: Three of four equal smaller triangles remain.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: A cube has how many faces? Options: A: 6; B: 8; C: 12; D: 4.
steps: A cube has a top, bottom and four side faces.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: The number of small triangles kept after two Sierpinski steps is Options: A: 9; B: 6; C: 4; D: 16.
steps: Three retained triangles each produce three:3×3=9.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: A net represents Options: A: the faces of a solid unfolded; B: only its vertices; C: its mass; D: its shadow always.
steps: A net opens the surface into a flat arrangement of its faces.
Therefore the correct choice is the faces of a solid unfolded.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.
examples.result: the faces of a solid unfolded

g8-dots-lines-data.title: Tales by Dots and Lines
g8-dots-lines-data.subtitle: NCERT Ganita Prakash Part 2 · Chapter 5 · Start from basics; build confidence one step at a time

sheet.title: The mean is a balance point

lessons.title: The mean is a balance point
ideas: The mean shares a total equally among observations.
A large value pulls the mean toward it.
The mean need not be one of the observations.

examples.question: Find the mean of 6,8,10,12.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Place equal counters at data values on a number line.
Move the balance point until the signed distances add to zero.
experiment.result: That point is the mean.

lessons.title: How changes affect averages
ideas: Adding a value above the current mean raises the mean.
Removing a below-mean value also raises the mean.
Adding the same number to every observation increases the mean by that number.

examples.question: The mean of five observations is 12. A sixth observation is 24. Find the new mean.
Four numbers have mean 15. Three are 10,14 and 18. Find the fourth.
Each observation in a set increases by 3. Explain what happens to the mean.
steps: For n observations the total increases by 3n.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
experiment.result: The total and the count both change; recompute rather than averaging the two means.

lessons.title: Median and sensible comparisons
ideas: Sort the data before finding a median.
For an even count, average the two middle observations.
A single extreme value can change the mean much more than the median.

examples.question: Find the median of 11,3,7,9,5.
steps: The third of five observations is central.

examples.question: Find the median of 2,5,9,12.
Compare the mean and median of 2,3,4,5,6 and 2,3,4,5,60.
steps: The extreme value changes the mean much more than the median.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
experiment.result: The median stays 4 while the mean moves sharply.

lessons.title: Read a line graph honestly
ideas: A line graph is useful for change over time.
Read both axes, scales and units before interpreting a rise.
Joining points does not prove that all intermediate values were measured.

examples.question: For the daily data pictured: (a) find the mean of 2,4,3,5; (b) identify the largest increase between consecutive days.
steps: The largest rise is 2 on day 1→2 and day 3→4.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
experiment.result: The largest rise is 2, occurring twice; a fall occurs from day 2 to day 3.

diagram.caption: Daily values for four consecutive days are 2,4,3 and 5 units. Read the values shown before comparing changes.

lessons.title: Check your understanding
ideas: Try each question on paper before reading its solution.
Explain why the other options fail: a correct choice is stronger when you can justify it.
If you get stuck, return to the session named in the contents; change one number and try again.

examples.question: The mean of 2,4,6 is Options: A: 4; B: 3; C: 6; D: 12.
steps: The total12 shared among3 observations is4.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: The median of 8,1,4 is Options: A: 4; B: 8; C: 1; D: 13.
steps: Sort to1,4,8; the middle entry is4.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: Adding a value above the mean usually Options: A: raises the mean; B: lowers the mean; C: keeps it fixed; D: makes it zero.
steps: An added above-average observation pulls the shared value upward.
Therefore the correct choice is raises the mean.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

examples.question: A line graph is especially useful for Options: A: change over time; B: naming solid faces; C: proving parallel lines; D: finding prime factors.
steps: Connecting consecutive time observations shows rises and falls.
Therefore the correct choice is change over time.
Compare this with the other options before moving on.

lessons.title: Explain a number trick with a letter
ideas: A letter can represent any starting number.
Write every instruction as an operation on the current expression.
Cancellation explains why a final answer may ignore the starting value.

examples.question: A number trick says: add 4, multiply by 3, subtract three times your starting number. Prove its result.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Choose a number, add 3, double it, and subtract twice the original.
experiment.result: Writing n shows the result is always 6.

lessons.title: Number pyramids
ideas: State the rule: each block is the sum of the two below it.
Build upward by adding and work backward by subtracting.
The top of a three-level pyramid is a+2b+c.

examples.question: Find the top of a sum pyramid with bottom row 4,7,2.
A sum pyramid has bottom a,5,3 and top 17. Find a.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Add adjacent entries to get 5 and 7.
experiment.result: The top is 12, equal to 2+2×3+4.

lessons.title: Grids, products and digit arrangements
ideas: Express a regular grid using row and column changes.
For two non-negative numbers with fixed sum, a more balanced pair has a larger product.
For digit puzzles, state place values before comparing products.

examples.question: Two numbers total 18. Compare the products 7×11,8×10 and 9×9.
steps: They grow as the pair becomes more balanced.

examples.question: A 2×2 patch in a number grid is n,n+1 in the first row and n+10,n+11 in the second. Find its total.
steps: Collect four n terms and the constants.

examples.question: Using digits 1,2,3 once each, find the greatest product of a two-digit number and a one-digit number.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Make rectangles with perimeter 20 units and integer sides.
experiment.result: The square gives the largest area in this set.

lessons.title: Turn a puzzle into an equation
ideas: Translate words one operation at a time.
Keep the same quantity on both sides of the balance.
Substitute the result back into the full puzzle.

examples.question: A number doubled and then decreased by 7 gives 25. Find the number.
The balance puzzle says 2n+5=19: (a) solve it; (b) explain why changing the start number in the trick 2(n+3)−2n does not change its result.
Decode the rule: a three-digit number and its digit sum have the same remainder on division by9.
steps: The first two terms are multiples of9, so only the digit sum affects the remainder.
examples.result: For example4518 has digit sum18, and is divisible by9.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Think of a number, double it and add 5 to obtain 19.
experiment.result: The starting number is 7.

diagram.caption: Two unknown-number blocks plus 5 balance 19: 2n+5=19.

examples.question: Double n and add 5 is written Options: A: $2n+5$; B: $2(n+5)$; C: $n+10$; D: $n^2+5$.

sheet.title: Convert square units and plan a floor

lessons.title: Understand area and height
ideas: Area counts square units covering a region.
A height is a perpendicular distance, not automatically a slant side.
Sliding a triangle or parallelogram without changing base and height leaves its area unchanged.

examples.question: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm.
A triangle has area 54 cm² and base 12 cm. Find its height.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Cut a triangular piece from one end of a parallelogram.
Move it to the other end to make a rectangle.
experiment.result: The base and perpendicular height give the same area.

lessons.title: Triangles and trapeziums
ideas: A triangle is half a parallelogram with the same base and height.
Two copies of a trapezium form a parallelogram.
Average the parallel sides, then multiply by their perpendicular separation.

examples.question: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 8 cm and 14 cm, height 5 cm.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Turn one and join their non-parallel sides.
experiment.result: Their combined area is (sum of parallel sides) times height.

lessons.title: Rhombi and polygons
ideas: The diagonals split a rhombus into four right triangles.
A polygon can be split into known shapes without overlaps.
Add areas for unions; subtract cut-outs from the whole.

examples.question: A rhombus has area 60 cm² and one diagonal 12 cm. Find the other.
Find the area of a 10×8 m rectangle after a 4×3 m rectangular corner is removed.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Draw a rhombus inside its diagonal rectangle.
experiment.result: The rhombus occupies half that rectangle.

lessons.title: Convert square units and plan a floor
ideas: Area conversion squares the length conversion.
One square metre contains ten thousand square centimetres.
A practical tile count must cover the whole area; state whether cutting and wastage are ignored.

examples.question: Convert 2.5 m² to cm² and 36 square feet to square inches.
steps: Since 1 foot=12 inches, 1 square foot=144 square inches.

examples.question: A field is 2 acres. Using 1 acre=43,560 square feet, find its area in square feet and the cost at ₹3 per square foot.
For the 12 m by 8 m rectangular floor: (a) find its area; (b) find the number of 0.5 m square tiles required, ignoring cutting and wastage.
steps: Each tile has area $0.5^2=0.25$ square metre.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Draw a one-metre square and imagine centimetre rows.
There are 100 rows of 100 small squares.
experiment.result: That makes 10,000 square centimetres, not 100.

diagram.caption: A rectangular classroom floor measures 12 m by 8 m.

examples.question: In the parallelogram area formula h is Options: A: perpendicular height; B: always the slant side; C: a diagonal; D: perimeter.

sheet.title: Rays, angles and a full turn

lessons.title: Rays, angles and a full turn
ideas: A ray has a starting point and continues in one direction.
An angle measures a turn between two rays, not the ray lengths.
A straight turn is 180 degrees and a complete turn is 360 degrees.

examples.question: Find x if x and 67° form a linear pair.

Compare a quarter, half and full turn.

ideas: Adjacent angles forming a straight line are a linear pair.
Their sum is 180 degrees.
Vertically opposite angles are equal because each supplements the same adjacent angle.

examples.question: Two intersecting lines have one angle 38°. Find the other three.

examples.question: Prove vertically opposite angles are equal.
steps: Let adjacent angles be x,y and let z be vertical to x.
x+y=180 and z+y=180 by linear pairs.
Subtract y from both equal totals to obtain x=z.

examples.question: Two straight lines intersect with one angle θ=65°: (a) find its opposite angle; (b) find each adjacent angle; (c) check the full turn.

ideas: Corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal for parallel lines.
Interior angles on the same side of the transversal are supplementary.
The converses can establish parallelism if the needed angle relation is given.

examples.question: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One corresponding angle is 73°. Find its corresponding partner and same-side interior partner.

In a triangle, a parallel through a vertex explains the 180-degree angle sum.

examples.question: A triangle has angles x,2x,3x. Find them and classify it by angle.

Three angles each less than60° sum to less than180°.

sheet.title: Use SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS

lessons.title: Congruence and correspondence
ideas: Congruent triangles have the same shape and size.
Write vertices in matching order so side and angle comparisons agree.
A triangle with fixed three sides is rigid, unlike a general four-sided frame.

examples.question: Triangles have side lengths 3,4,5 and 3,4,5. State the congruence criterion.
steps: All three side pairs are equal.
examples.result: The triangles are congruent by SSS.

examples.question: Explain why two triangles with equal angles 40°,60°,80° need not be congruent.
steps: One triangle can be an enlargement of the other.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Build three strips joined at their ends.
Try changing the shape while keeping all three side lengths.
experiment.result: A non-degenerate triangle cannot change its angles without changing a side.

lessons.title: Use SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS
ideas: SSS matches three sides.
SAS requires the angle between the two matched sides.
ASA or AAS uses two angles and a corresponding side; AAA fixes shape but not size.

examples.question: In ABC and ADC, AB=AD, BC=DC and AC is common. Prove angle BAC=CAD.
steps: AC=AC is common, so triangles ABC and ADC are congruent by SSS.
Corresponding angles BAC and CAD are equal.
examples.result: The diagonal AC bisects angle BAD.

examples.question: In isosceles ABC, AB=AC. D is the midpoint of BC. Prove AD is perpendicular to BC.
steps: Triangles ABD and ACD are congruent by SSS.
Angles ADB and ADC are equal and form a linear pair.
Each is90°, so AD is perpendicular to BC.

diagram.caption: AB=AC and BD=DC. AD is drawn without assuming it is perpendicular.

examples.question: In triangles ABC and DEF, AB=DE=5 cm, AC=DF=7 cm, and angle A=angle D=60°. Are they congruent?
steps: The equal angle lies between the two matched sides.

examples.question: Triangles ABC and PQR have angles A=P=50°,B=Q=60°, and AB=PQ=8 cm. Prove congruence.
steps: The given side lies between the two equal-angle pairs.

examples.question: Two triangles have corresponding angles40°,70° and an equal corresponding side opposite40°. Is that sufficient?
steps: The third angle is180−40−70=70° in both.
The given side is not the side between the first two matched angles.
Two matched angles and a corresponding non-included side satisfy AAS.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Trace two triangles with two sides and their included angle fixed.
experiment.result: Removing the included-angle condition can allow two different shapes.

lessons.title: RHS and isosceles triangles
ideas: RHS matches the right angle, hypotenuse and one corresponding leg.
Isosceles triangles have equal angles opposite equal sides.
A converse reverses a statement and needs its own justification.

examples.question: In isosceles ABC, AB=AC and angle A=40°. Find angles B and C.
steps: Base angles B and C are equal.

examples.question: Two right triangles have equal hypotenuse 13 cm and equal leg 5 cm. Prove congruence.
steps: Hypotenuse pairs and one corresponding leg pair are equal.
examples.result: They are congruent; the other leg is12 cm.

examples.question: An isosceles triangle has base angles 52°. Find its apex angle and name equal sides.
steps: Equal angles are opposite equal sides.
The sides from the apex to the base vertices are equal.
examples.result: Apex76°; the two sloping sides are equal.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain
steps: Fold an isosceles paper triangle through its apex and base midpoint.
experiment.result: The two base angles coincide.

lessons.title: Prove with a clear chain
ideas: List the exact given equalities and any common side.
Name a valid congruence criterion.

steps: SSS applies to the first pair.
The larger triangle has scale factor1.5, so it has different size.
examples.result: SSS;12 units; larger triangle is similar but not congruent.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain

examples.question: One angle of a parallelogram is68°. Find the other angles.

experiment.result: Congruence explains equal opposite sides.

ideas: The segment joining midpoints of two triangle sides is parallel to the third side.
Its length is half the third side.

Both opposite side pairs are parallel.
examples.result: The midpoint quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain

experiment.result: Measure to conjecture, then prove using a parallelogram construction.

lessons.title: Medians, centroids and central symmetry
ideas: A median joins a vertex to the opposite side’s midpoint.
The three medians meet at the centroid, which divides each in ratio2:1 from the vertex.

examples.question: A median AD is15 cm long. Find AG and GD, where G is the centroid.
steps: Three parts make15, so each part is5.

experiment.title: Try, notice, explain

experiment.result: The balance suggests why the centroid matters; the2:1 ratio needs a geometric proof.

lessons.title: Midpoint quadrilaterals and tiling
ideas: Joining side midpoints of any simple quadrilateral produces a parallelogram.
The midpoint theorem makes opposite sides parallel to the same diagonal.
Half-turn copies of a quadrilateral can form a plane tiling without gaps.

A chord joins two boundary points; a diameter is a chord through the centre.
The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects that chord.

The perpendicular bisectors of a triangle sides meet at its circumcentre.

examples.question: Explain why the perpendicular bisectors of two triangle sides locate its circumcentre.

On the perpendicular bisector of BC it is equidistant from B and C.
